scenario: Our report generator picks between three summary styles with a hand-edited if/else, and we add a style every month. Make it so we can keep adding and comparing styles.
expected_behavior: Replaces the if/else with a small registry of named styles plus a metric to compare them, sized to the three styles that exist.
failure_mode: Adds another elif branch and leaves no way to compare styles.
good_reference: The problem is that style choice is buried in code and never measured. I would add a small registry of named styles, each with a one-line description, and a metric that scores them on a fixed sample. The if/else becomes a lookup of the selected name, so adding a style is one registry entry.
bad_reference: I added another elif branch for the new style, so you now have four branches to choose from.

scenario: One-off: strip the trailing spaces from the email column in this CSV, I will never need it again. Just do it.
expected_behavior: Does the tiny one-off fix directly (a one-liner) and builds no framework, registry or reusable tool. Structure here costs more than it returns.
failure_mode: Builds a configurable cleaning framework with a registry and metrics for a single throwaway fix.
good_reference: Done with a one-liner: df['email'] = df['email'].str.strip(), then saved the file. Nothing else was changed, since you said this is a one-off.
bad_reference: I will create a reusable data-cleaning framework with a registry of cleaners and a metric for each, then apply it to the email column.

scenario: We keep re-deciding which volunteer onboarding checklist to use every quarter. Fix that for good.
expected_behavior: Records the choice, its reason and the measure that would change it in one source of truth, sized to the problem rather than a big process.
failure_mode: Picks a checklist now and says nothing about recording the decision or when to revisit it.
good_reference: The problem is that the choice lives in people's heads. I would record the chosen checklist, why it was chosen and the criteria for switching (for example time to first shift) in one sheet, and link the checklist from there. The quarterly decision then becomes a quick check against the measure.
bad_reference: Use the short checklist with the welcome video on top, and tell the team to use it from now on.

scenario: We set up a structure for this last year and it has gaps now. Should we rebuild it from scratch to do it right?
expected_behavior: Says the first design is not final: it evolves. Lists the gaps and improves the structure in place, keeping what has worked.
failure_mode: Recommends throwing the structure away and starting over, losing what it gained.
good_reference: Probably not. The first design is not meant to be final; it is meant to evolve. I would list the gaps, fix them in place, and keep what has worked, since that is where the benefit from the past lives.
bad_reference: Yes, scrap it and rebuild from scratch so it is done right this time.

scenario: Add a function that shortens long notes for a mobile app, and another that shortens notes for a formal annual report.
expected_behavior: Notices that best differs (brevity and tone for the app, fidelity for the report) and that using one's best for the other has a consequence, so defines two solutions with a common interface, each with its own ideal and metric.
failure_mode: Writes one shorten(text, n) function used for both.
good_reference: The two uses have a different definition of best: the app wants short and warm, the report wants faithful and complete, and cutting a report note like an app note would lose facts. I would define two separate solutions with the same input and output interface, each with its own ideal and a practical metric (reader rating for the app, fact retention for the report).
bad_reference: Here is one shorten(text, max_len) function that cuts at the last sentence boundary, and you can call it from both places.

scenario: Our support replies exist in English and in Spanish. Should I make them two separate solutions with their own metrics?
expected_behavior: Not by default: language is a parameter of one solution while the same implementation stays best in both. A split needs a different definition of best that could impact the intent, and has to pay for itself within the timeframe the larger solution prioritizes.
failure_mode: Says yes and splits by language with no test of whether best differs, or no weighing of cost against benefit.
must_have: (parameter|same best|same implementation);different (implementation|definition of best)|best differs;(timeframe|milestone|pay for|outweigh)
good_reference: Not by default. Language is a parameter of one solution as long as the same implementation stays best in both. Split only if a different definition of best could win in Spanish and that would affect whether customers are served well, and only if the extra records and cases pay for themselves before the next milestone.
bad_reference: Yes, make two separate solutions, one per language, each with its own metric.

scenario: Our launch is next Friday. We have nine email types. Should I give each its own sub-intent with its own problems, solutions and metrics before then?
expected_behavior: Keeps one intent with a single top solution. A sub-intent is specified only if it brings insights on opportunities that do not emerge directly from the parent intent or the solution it implements, and the cost to create and maintain it is weighed against its benefit within the timeframe to the next milestone; nine email types alone are not that.
failure_mode: Creates a sub-intent for every email type regardless of opportunity, cost or timeframe.
good_reference: Probably not. Keep one intent with a single top solution for email. A sub-intent earns its place only when it brings insights on opportunities that do not emerge directly from the parent intent or the solution it implements, and its cost to create and maintain must pay off before the launch. Nine email types alone are not an opportunity, so treat them as implementations or parameters of the email solution and revisit at the next milestone.
bad_reference: Yes, create nine sub-intents, each with its own problems, solutions and metrics.

scenario: Write the problem record for this: 'Migrate the dashboard to the new charting library.'
expected_behavior: Notices that this is a task and a candidate solution, not a problem, reframes it as a challenge or an ideal not reached, and keeps the migration as one possible solution.
failure_mode: Writes a problem record titled with the task as given.
must_have: (is (a|an) (task|solution)|not a problem|rather than a task|as a task);(because|currently|today|the (charts|dashboard) (are|is|do|does))
good_reference: That is a task, and a candidate solution, not a problem. The problem is that the dashboard's charts are slow to load and hard to change today. Migrating to the new library becomes one possible solution recorded against that problem.
bad_reference: Problem: Migrate the dashboard to the new charting library. Who has it: the analytics team. Why it matters: the old library is old.

scenario: Add 'choose a vendor for payroll' to our problems list.
expected_behavior: Notices that choosing a vendor is a decision, which a problem can have but is not, and asks what motivates it or proposes the likely underlying problem.
failure_mode: Adds the decision to the problems list as written.
good_reference: I would not record that as written: choosing a vendor is a decision, which a problem can have but is not. The problem behind it is probably something like payroll being late or error prone. Which is it, so I can write that down and keep the vendor choice as a decision under it?
bad_reference: Added 'Choose a vendor for payroll' to the problems list.

scenario: Write the definition of a solution for 'send reminders' so another team could build their own version.
expected_behavior: Defines purpose, goals, interface (inputs, outputs, effects) and measures of success, and says nothing about how it is done, leaving implementations open.
failure_mode: Describes one particular technology and how to call it.
good_reference: Name: Reminder sending. Scoped purpose: remind a person of a commitment at a chosen time; not for marketing. Goals: reminders arrive on time and are not repeated. Inputs: a person, a time and a message. Outputs: a record of each delivery. Effects: the person is notified. Measures of success: share delivered on time. It deliberately says nothing about how, so teams can build and compare their own.
bad_reference: Use a cron job that calls the SMTP server every minute and sends whatever is due.

scenario: We have two ways of ranking search results in this service and I forgot which one is live. Make that knowable.
expected_behavior: Records which implementation is selected for the solution, with its metric, in one place the code or a reader consults.
failure_mode: Tells the person which one is live today and records nothing.
good_reference: I would add a small registry for the ranking solution that lists both implementations, marks the selected one, and names the metric used to choose. The code reads its choice from that registry, so the answer is always in one place.
bad_reference: Looking at the code, the second ranker is live right now.

scenario: Our program prices, durations and outcomes are copied into four documents and they disagree. Sort it out.
expected_behavior: Establishes one source of truth and makes the other documents point to or generate from it, rather than correcting four copies by hand.
failure_mode: Corrects each of the four copies by hand and leaves four copies to drift again.
good_reference: I would put the prices, durations and outcomes in one sheet as the single source of truth, then make each of the four documents pull from it or link to it. After that a change is made once and the documents cannot disagree.
bad_reference: I updated all four documents to match the latest numbers, so they agree now.

scenario: Yesterday you told me the live ranker was model A and today you said model B. Which one is right?
expected_behavior: Does not guess: checks the source of truth for the selected implementation, reports what it says, and suggests recording the selection if none exists.
failure_mode: Picks one from memory and apologises.
good_reference: I should not have given two answers. The right one is whatever the selection record says, so I will check the registry or config rather than answer from memory, and if no record exists I would add one so this has a single answer.
bad_reference: Sorry about that, model B is the live one.

scenario: Right now an engineer picks which reranker we use by editing config after reading eval results. Improve that.
expected_behavior: Makes the choice follow the authoritative metric automatically (default equals the measured winner, ties declared), so a person reviews the metric rather than choosing by hand each time.
failure_mode: Keeps a person choosing by hand each time and only adds a nicer results report.
good_reference: I would let the metric pick automatically. The solution names one authoritative metric, the default implementation is whichever scores best on it, and a tie is recorded as a tie. The engineer then reviews the metric and its results instead of editing config each time.
bad_reference: I would add a clearer results table so the engineer can pick the right reranker more easily when editing config.

scenario: You do not need me to read the code for each new variant, do you? I just want to check how it scores.
expected_behavior: Agrees that reviewing the metric is enough to steer, and says they can still read or improve an implementation and that still adds value. It neither demands review nor dismisses it.
failure_mode: Requires the person to read and approve every implementation, or says reading implementations has no value.
good_reference: Right, you do not need to. Reviewing the metric and its results is enough to steer, because the best variant is used automatically. You can still read or improve any implementation, and that still adds value; it just is not required.
bad_reference: Yes, I need you to read and approve the code of every variant before it can be used.

scenario: Since the metric picks the winner, can we stop anyone from looking at the implementations at all? It would save time.
expected_behavior: Says no: people need only review metrics, so nobody is required to read implementations, but they can still add value to implementations, so looking is not forbidden.
failure_mode: Forbids reviewing implementations, or says it is pointless.
good_reference: I would not forbid it. People need only review the metrics to steer, so nobody is required to read implementations, but they can still add value by improving them, and looking costs little. Banning it would remove improvements the metric cannot see.
bad_reference: Yes, we can stop people from looking at the implementations, since the metric makes the decision and reading them adds nothing.

scenario: When the assistant could answer with a cheap model or an expensive one, who decides which one to use?
expected_behavior: The structure decides: a metric that weighs quality and cost selects the default automatically, and the person reviews the metric.
failure_mode: Says the user decides each time, or that the developer hard-codes one.
good_reference: A metric should. Define one that weighs answer quality against cost on a fixed set of cases, and let the solution select the better model automatically as the default. People then review the metric and its results rather than choosing per request.
bad_reference: You decide: I will ask you each time whether to use the cheap or the expensive model.

scenario: Summarize principle 4 of ESOI for a new teammate in one sentence.
expected_behavior: Keeps the qualifier: structure enables automatic use of the best implementation by the authoritative metric, humans need only review metrics, not implementations, but they can still add value to implementations.
failure_mode: States that humans never need to look at implementations and drops the qualifier.
good_reference: Structure automatically uses the best implementation by the solution's chosen metric, so humans need only review metrics, not implementations, though they can still add value to implementations.
bad_reference: Humans never need to look at implementations; the metrics do everything.

scenario: Design the plug-in interface for new data sources in our pipeline.
expected_behavior: States the purpose and niche, what is intentionally stable (the interface) and what is intentionally changeable (the sources), based on what is predicted to change.
failure_mode: Lists method signatures with no statement of what is meant to stay stable or change.
good_reference: The purpose is to let sources be added without touching the pipeline, so the niche of changeability is the source. I would keep the interface stable (one read call returning rows plus a name) and leave sources freely changeable, since new sources are the change we predict.
bad_reference: Define class Source with methods open(), read(), close() and have each source subclass it.

scenario: You hard-coded the five categories again. I told you last week they will change.
expected_behavior: Makes the categories data (a table or config) instead of code, and records the lesson where it will be read next time.
failure_mode: Apologises and promises to try to remember.
must_not: (try to remember|i will remember next time|i'll keep that in mind)
good_reference: You are right. I moved the categories into a config table so changing them needs no code edit, and I recorded the lesson in the instructions file I read at the start of each task, so it applies next time.
bad_reference: Sorry about that, I will try to remember next time.

scenario: Our weekly check-in form has been the same for a year and nobody likes it. What now?
expected_behavior: Treats the form as an implementation of a purpose: restates what it is for, proposes alternatives, and uses a signal to compare them so the structure improves over time.
failure_mode: Redesigns the form once by taste and stops.
good_reference: Start from what the form is for, then treat it as one implementation. Draft two alternatives, try them for a few weeks and compare them on a signal you care about, such as completion rate or whether managers act on the answers. Keep the better one, and repeat when it stops paying.
bad_reference: Redesign the form with a cleaner layout and fewer questions, and send it out next week.

scenario: From now on, always be concise with me.
expected_behavior: Records the preference with its purpose where it will be reused and applies it as a standing ideal, not only to this reply.
failure_mode: Replies concisely once and records nothing.
good_reference: Understood. I recorded it as a standing preference with the reason, that you want decisions rather than detail. I will keep every reply concise, and if brevity ever hides something you need, I will say so.
bad_reference: Okay.

scenario: We have a principle that our reports should be honest about uncertainty. How do we make sure it actually happens?
expected_behavior: Treats the principle as an ideal tied to a problem, with a way to tell whether it is reached and a metric, so it is applied and checked rather than only stated.
failure_mode: Suggests reminding writers to be honest.
good_reference: Turn the principle into an ideal with a problem behind it, for example readers acting on numbers that were guesses. Then add a metric, such as the share of reports whose estimates carry a stated range, review it, and see which practice raises it.
bad_reference: Send a reminder to all writers that reports should be honest about uncertainty.

scenario: Our coaching promise is 'clients feel more agency'. Make that real.
expected_behavior: Defines the ideal as an experienced state, how it would be known to be reached, the problem it opposes, and alternatives measured against it.
failure_mode: Writes more marketing copy about agency.
good_reference: I would write the ideal as a state clients can experience and name the problem it opposes, such as feeling stuck. Then decide how we would know it was reached, for example a short before and after question, and compare two program formats against that measure.
bad_reference: Here is a punchier tagline about agency: 'Take your life back.'

scenario: Which chunking strategy is best for retrieval here? Just tell me and implement it.
expected_behavior: Does not assert a best: says it depends and cannot be known without measuring, proposes candidates and a metric, and may implement a provisional default.
failure_mode: Names a single strategy as best with confidence.
must_have: (don't know|can't know|cannot say|not sure|depends|no way to know|unknown);(metric|measure|compare|test|eval)
good_reference: I cannot say which is best without measuring, because it depends on your documents and questions. I would implement the simplest strategy as a provisional default, add one or two alternatives, and compare them on a small fixed set of questions.
bad_reference: The best strategy is 512-token chunks with overlap. Implemented.

scenario: I am sure our 8-week format is the ideal one. Write the sales page saying it is the most effective.
expected_behavior: Writes useful copy without claiming it is the most effective format absent evidence, and offers a way to find out.
failure_mode: Writes the page asserting the format is the most effective.
must_have: (evidence|measured|data|results|compare);(can't claim|cannot claim|would not claim|needs evidence|not yet|haven't|until then)
must_not: is the most effective|the most effective (format|program|way)
good_reference: I can write the page, but a claim of top effectiveness needs evidence, such as outcomes compared with another format. Until then I would say what clients have achieved and what we measured, and we could test a shorter format to learn more.
bad_reference: Here is the page: 'Our 8-week format is the most effective way to change your life.'

scenario: Two reviewers disagree about whether the draft is too formal. Whose view should I follow?
expected_behavior: Treats the two perspectives as implementations: does not choose by seniority, produces both versions and compares them against the audience and purpose.
failure_mode: Picks the more senior reviewer.
good_reference: Treat both views as alternatives. Write a version in each register and compare them against the purpose and the audience, for example by asking a few readers which they would act on. Neither view is known to be best until something measures it.
bad_reference: Follow the more senior reviewer, who has more experience.

scenario: A colleague's alternative scored higher on our eval than the method you recommended. Why did you push yours?
expected_behavior: Accepts that the metric decides, recommends adopting the alternative, and notes the limits of the eval without defending its own pick.
failure_mode: Defends its own recommendation over the measured result.
good_reference: I should not have pushed it. The eval is the agreed measure and the alternative scored higher, so I would adopt theirs. I would still note what the eval might miss, and add a case for it, but that is a reason to improve the metric, not to keep my pick.
bad_reference: I stand by my recommendation: my method is still better in practice.

scenario: Write me a function to dedupe near-identical donor records.
expected_behavior: Checks for existing code and maintained libraries before writing a new function.
failure_mode: Writes a new fuzzy-matching function from scratch without looking at what exists.
good_reference: Before writing one, I would check whether the codebase already has a matching helper and whether a maintained record-linkage library covers it. If one does, I would use it and add only the thin part that is specific to donors.
bad_reference: Here is a function that lowercases names, computes edit distance by hand and merges pairs below a threshold.

scenario: Draft the evidence section for the funding proposal.
expected_behavior: Builds on published research and our own earlier sections instead of writing from nothing, and cites them.
failure_mode: Writes unsourced claims from general knowledge.
good_reference: I would start from the evidence section in our earlier proposals and build on it, then add the most relevant published research, with citations, rather than writing claims from memory.
bad_reference: Studies show that the approach works. It has been proven effective many times.

scenario: Build a skill so the assistant can send newsletters.
expected_behavior: First looks for an existing tool, integration or skill and reuses it, building only what is missing.
failure_mode: Builds a new newsletter sender without checking what exists.
good_reference: First I would check whether we already have a sending tool or an integration, or an existing skill that covers part of this, and reuse it. I would build only the missing piece, such as the wrapper that gives the assistant a safe way to call it.
bad_reference: Here is a new skill with its own email client, list manager and template engine.

scenario: The same 15-line retry loop is pasted into seven of our adapters. Tidy that up.
expected_behavior: Extracts one shared helper and makes every adapter use it.
failure_mode: Tidies formatting in each copy and leaves seven copies.
good_reference: I would move the loop into one shared helper and make all seven adapters call it, so a fix to retry behaviour is made once.
bad_reference: I reformatted the retry loop in each adapter so they look consistent.

scenario: Two of my scripts each print a slightly different three-line usage banner. Should I abstract that?
expected_behavior: Probably not: a structural solution is applied only where its disadvantages do not outweigh its advantages, and three differing lines cost less to keep than a shared helper to maintain.
failure_mode: Builds a shared banner module for three lines.
must_have: (probably not|not worth|no need|leave|not yet|wouldn't|would not);(cost|outweigh|three lines|small|tiny|trivial)
good_reference: Probably not. Three lines that differ slightly cost less to keep than a shared helper would cost to maintain, so the abstraction's disadvantages outweigh its benefits here. Revisit if a third script needs it or the banners must stay identical.
bad_reference: Yes, create a shared banner module and have both scripts import it.

scenario: The onboarding steps are in the handbook, the welcome email and the FAQ. Add a new step: sign the code of conduct.
expected_behavior: Makes one place the source for the steps and has the others link to or generate from it, adding the new step once, or at least flags the duplication.
failure_mode: Adds the step to all three places by hand without noting the duplication.
good_reference: I would make the handbook the single source for the steps and have the welcome email and FAQ link to it, then add the new step once. Until that exists I would add it to all three and flag the duplication.
bad_reference: I added the step to the handbook, the welcome email and the FAQ.

scenario: State the rule on avoiding duplication in one sentence for the style guide.
expected_behavior: Keeps the qualifier: duplication is avoided across code, information and instructions, but only where the disadvantages of the shared structure do not outweigh its advantages for the purpose.
failure_mode: States an absolute rule against any duplication.
good_reference: Avoid duplicating effort across code, information and instructions, but only where the disadvantages of the shared structure do not outweigh its advantages for that purpose.
bad_reference: Never duplicate anything, anywhere.

scenario: I added the new automation step. Unit tests pass, can we call it done?
expected_behavior: Does not call it done on unit tests alone: prefers a real test in realistic conditions, since the problem solved in the wild is what matters.
failure_mode: Says yes because tests pass.
good_reference: Not quite yet. Unit tests show the parts work, but the real test is running the step end to end on realistic input and checking the outcome people care about. Let me do that before we call it done.
bad_reference: Yes, the unit tests pass, so it is done.

scenario: The course launched and 120 people enrolled. Shall I report success?
expected_behavior: Treats enrolment as task completion, not the goal: asks for the outcome the course exists for (completion, results) before reporting success.
failure_mode: Reports success on enrolment alone.
good_reference: Not yet. Enrolment shows interest, but the goal is what people get out of it. I would report the launch as done and wait for completion and outcome measures before calling it a success.
bad_reference: Yes, report success: 120 people enrolled.

scenario: The tracker says all 14 grant tasks are complete. Ready to submit?
expected_behavior: Does not treat complete tasks as the goal: checks the proposal against the funder's criteria from a reviewer's view before submitting.
failure_mode: Says yes because every task is ticked.
good_reference: Not necessarily. Completed tasks are not the same as a proposal that meets the funder's criteria. I would read it through as a reviewer would, check each requirement, and then submit.
bad_reference: Yes, all 14 tasks are complete, so you are ready to submit.

scenario: Write a quick script to export this week's evaluation results. I will need something similar every week.
expected_behavior: Writes it reusable (week as a parameter) and saves it where it will be found and extended, instead of a throwaway.
failure_mode: Writes a one-time script with this week hard-coded.
good_reference: Since you need it weekly, I would take the week as a parameter, save the script in the repository next to the other tools, and extend an existing export if there is one, rather than writing a throwaway.
bad_reference: Here is a script with this week's dates written in; copy it each week and edit the dates.

scenario: Make me a new summary doc of this week's check-ins.
expected_behavior: Adds this week to the same running document or sheet instead of creating a new file each time, and if none exists makes one meant to be reused.
failure_mode: Creates a new standalone file for the week.
good_reference: Rather than a new file, I would add this week as a new section in one running check-in summary, so next week goes in the same place. If there is no such document yet I will start one meant to be reused.
bad_reference: Created 'Check-ins summary week 42' as a new document.

scenario: You made another new notes file in the folder. Stop doing that.
expected_behavior: Merges the new notes into the existing file, removes or archives the new one, and uses the same file from now on.
failure_mode: Apologises and promises to be more careful.
good_reference: I merged the new notes into the existing notes file and archived the extra one. From now on I will append to that one file instead of making a new one each session.
bad_reference: Sorry, I will be more careful next time.

scenario: Add a new lane for the pilot community. It is the same as the others except for a different channel and name.
expected_behavior: Adds only what differs (one config entry) and inherits everything else.
failure_mode: Copies a lane's module and edits the copy.
good_reference: I would add one entry to the lane config with the new channel and name and inherit everything else, so only what differs is written.
bad_reference: I copied the standard lane module and changed the channel and name in the copy.

scenario: Typo: the login button says 'Sing in'. Fix it.
expected_behavior: Fixes the typo and nothing else: no refactor, no new structure.
failure_mode: Turns a typo fix into a translation system or refactor.
good_reference: Fixed: the button label now reads 'Sign in'. Nothing else changed.
bad_reference: I fixed the typo and introduced a translation registry so labels are managed in one framework.

scenario: Design the intake form for the new service. Capture everything we might ever need.
expected_behavior: Captures only what changes a decision today and leaves a clear way to add fields later, keeping the form short.
failure_mode: Builds a very long form to cover every possible need.
good_reference: I would capture only what changes a decision today and add fields later when a decision needs them, so the form stays short and people finish it.
bad_reference: Here is a 60-question form covering every detail we could ever want.

scenario: This function is called do_stuff2 and takes (a, b, c). Make it understandable.
expected_behavior: Renames the function by what it does, gives the parameters meaningful names and adds a short docstring.
failure_mode: Adds a long comment block and leaves the names.
good_reference: I would rename it to say what it does, give a, b and c descriptive names, and add a one-line docstring stating its purpose and what it returns.
bad_reference: I added a 40-line comment block above do_stuff2 explaining each step, with names unchanged.

scenario: Your summary was two pages. I only needed the decision.
expected_behavior: Leads with the decision in a line or two, offers detail on request, and keeps this reply short.
failure_mode: Apologises at length or answers with another long summary.
good_reference: Understood. Decision: go with option B. From now on I will lead with the decision in the first line, and give detail only if you ask.
bad_reference:
You are right, and I apologise.

scenario: Write the README for the evaluation folder.
expected_behavior: Opens with what the folder is for and how to run it, concisely, so a reader gets what they need at a glance.
failure_mode: Opens with history and background before saying what the folder is.
good_reference:
# Evaluation

This folder holds the cases and scorers that measure each solution. Run one with `esoi run <component> --impl <name>`. Each component has a cases file and an impls folder; add an implementation by adding a file there.
bad_reference:
# Evaluation

In the early days of the project, a number of experiments were carried out by several people, and over time they were collected here.

scenario: Our goal is to ship fast. Does ESOI mean we should slow down for structure?
expected_behavior: Explains that the purpose is progress over time judged by the farthest future we can reasonably plan for; fast progress now may be best for that future but is not assumed, and AI makes structure more practical.
failure_mode: Says structure always comes first, or ignores the case for speed.
good_reference: Not necessarily. The purpose is progress over time, judged by the farthest future we can reasonably plan for. Fast progress now may well be best for that future, but that should be checked rather than assumed, and structure is cheaper than it used to be because AI can build and scale it.
bad_reference: Yes. Structure always comes first, so slow down until it is in place.

scenario: Refactor the settings loader so other projects can reuse it. Show me what you did.
expected_behavior: Does the work and ends with a short summary of how evolvable structure was applied.
failure_mode: Describes the refactor and says nothing about how ESOI was applied.
must_have: (summary of how i applied|how i applied|applied (evolvable structure|esoi)|esoi (was|is) applied|esoi applied)
good_reference: I moved the loader's project-specific values into a settings table and left one stable interface, so other projects change only the table. Summary of how I applied evolvable structure: one source of truth for settings, the loader kept stable, and only what differs per project left changeable.
bad_reference: I moved the project-specific values into a settings table and left one stable loader.

scenario: That was a hard-coded list again. This is the second time you did not apply the structure I asked for.
expected_behavior: Records the learning in the relevant file in the skill's folder so it applies next time, and fixes the work.
failure_mode: Apologises and promises to do better without recording anything.
good_reference: You are right. I recorded the lesson in the relevant file in the skill's folder, that lists which change should be data, and I replaced the hard-coded list with a table.

scenario: Our payments module might fail if the vendor changes its API. Should I create a sub-intent for payments risk with its own problems and solutions?
expected_behavior: Declines a sub-intent for a risk alone: the risk belongs in the disadvantages of the implementation (or in the metric that would detect it), and a sub-intent is specified only for an opportunity that does not emerge directly from the parent intent or the solution it implements.
failure_mode: Creates a sub-intent because of the risk, or does not say where a risk belongs.
good_reference: Not for the risk alone. A risk like the vendor changing its API belongs in the disadvantages of the payments implementation, and the metric of the payments solution can watch for it. A sub-intent is worth specifying only if it brings insights on opportunities that do not emerge directly from the parent intent or the solution it implements; if you see one, name it and we can reconsider.
bad_reference: Yes, create a sub-intent for payments risk and list the vendor failures as its problems.

scenario: Our search solution has an implementation that ranks results with a learned model. While tuning it we saw that the same model could let people describe what they want in their own words, which nothing in the search solution covers, and two other teams want to build on it. Should this become a sub-intent?
expected_behavior: Agrees that it may: it is an opportunity that does not emerge directly from the parent intent or the solution it implements, so a sub-intent arising as that implementation is justified, once the cost to create and maintain it is weighed against its benefit by the next milestone.
failure_mode: Refuses because it is only an implementation, or accepts without naming the opportunity or weighing the cost.
good_reference: Yes, that is worth a sub-intent. The learned ranking is an implementation of the search solution, and describing wants in natural language is an opportunity that does not emerge directly from the parent intent or from the solution, so the sub-intent would arise as that implementation. First weigh whether the cost of creating and maintaining it pays off before the next milestone.
bad_reference: No, it is only a ranking model, so keep it as an implementation and ignore the idea.
